paragraphs: It is a truth everyone accepts that a single man with a good fortune must be looking for a wife.

However little is known about such a man’s feelings or intentions when he first moves to a neighborhood, this idea is so firmly fixed in the minds of the surrounding families that he is regarded as the rightful property of one or another of their daughters.
“My dear Mr. Bennet,” his wife said to him one day, “have you heard that Netherfield Park has finally been rented?”
Mr. Bennet replied that he had not.
“But it has,” she answered. “Mrs. Long was just here, and she told me all about it.”
Mr. Bennet didn’t answer.
“Don’t you want to know who’s taken it?” his wife cried impatiently.
“You want to tell me, and I have no objection to hearing it.”
That was invitation enough.

“Well, my dear, you should know that Mrs. Long says Netherfield has been taken by a wealthy young man from the north of England. He came down on Monday in a carriage and four to see the place and was so delighted with it that he settled things with Mr. Morris right away. He’s to move in before Michaelmas, and some of his servants will be in the house by the end of next week.”
“What’s his name?”
“Bingley.”
“Is he married or single?”
“Oh, single, my dear, of course! A single man of large fortune: four or five thousand a year. What a fine thing for our girls!”
“How so? How can it affect them?”
“My dear Mr. Bennet,” his wife replied, “how can you be so tiresome? You must know I’m thinking of his marrying one of them.”
“Is that his plan in settling here?”
“Plan? Nonsense, how can you talk like that! But it’s very likely he’ll fall in love with one of them, and so you must visit him as soon as he arrives.”

“I don’t see the need. You and the girls can go, or you can send them on their own, which might be even better, because since you’re as good-looking as any of them, Mr. Bingley might like you best of the lot.”

“My dear, you flatter me. I certainly had my share of beauty once, but I don’t claim to be anything special now. When a woman has five grown daughters, she ought to stop thinking about her own looks.”
“In such cases, a woman usually doesn’t have much beauty left to think about.”
“But, my dear, you really must go and see Mr. Bingley when he comes to the neighborhood.”
“That’s more than I’ll promise, I assure you.”

“But think of your daughters. Just imagine what a match it would be for one of them. Sir William and Lady Lucas are determined to go, simply for that reason, because normally, you know, they don’t visit newcomers. You really must go, because it will be impossible for us to visit him if you don’t.”

“You’re being far too fussy. I’m sure Mr. Bingley will be very glad to see you, and I’ll send a few lines with you to assure him of my wholehearted consent to his marrying whichever of the girls he likes, though I must put in a good word for my little Lizzy.”
“I’d rather you did no such thing. Lizzy is no better than the others, and I’m sure she isn’t half as pretty as Jane or half as good-natured as Lydia. But you’re always favoring her.”
“None of them has much to recommend her,” he replied. “They’re all silly and ignorant, like other girls. But Lizzy has a bit more wit than her sisters.”
“Mr. Bennet, how can you insult your own children like that? You enjoy tormenting me. You have no pity for my poor nerves.”
“You misunderstand me, my dear. I have the highest respect for your nerves. They’re old friends of mine. I’ve heard you speak of them with concern for at least twenty years.”
“Ah, you don’t know what I suffer.”
“But I hope you’ll get over it and live to see many young men with four thousand a year move into the neighborhood.”
“It will do us no good if twenty of them come, since you won’t visit them.”
“You can depend on it, my dear, that when there are twenty, I’ll visit them all.”

Mr. Bennet was such an odd mixture of quick wit, sarcastic humor, reserve, and whim that twenty-three years of marriage had not been enough for his wife to understand his character. Her own mind was easier to read. She was a woman of poor understanding, little education, and unpredictable temper. When she was discontented, she imagined herself to be nervous. The business of her life was to get her daughters married, and her comfort was visiting and gossip.
